title: Pollyanna
author: Eleanor H. Porter
short_summary: Eleven-year-old Pollyanna Whittier, the daughter of a poor country minister, is orphaned and sent to live with her mother's sister, Aunt Polly, who takes her in out of duty and puts her in a bare attic room. Pollyanna has one inheritance from her father: the glad game, which began with a pair of crutches that arrived in a missionary barrel when she had asked for a doll. She plays it on an invalid who is never satisfied, an orphan boy nobody wants, a recluse with a broken leg and a discouraged minister — and then an automobile knocks her down, and the whole town has to play the game back at her.
extended_summary:
Pollyanna arrives in a New England town with one small trunk and nobody to meet her but the hired man. Aunt Polly Harrington is rich, unmarried and thoroughly dutiful: she says plainly that she is doing her duty, gives her niece the bare little room at the top of the house — no pictures, no carpet, no looking-glass — and forbids her to talk about her father. Pollyanna cries in the attic that first evening, and then finds something to be glad about: with no looking-glass she cannot see her freckles.

The glad game came from her father. One year the missionary barrel brought a pair of crutches instead of the doll she had asked for, and he told her to be glad she did not need them; after that they played it on everything. Pollyanna does not preach the game so much as leak it. Nancy the servant catches it first. Mrs. Snow, an invalid who always wanted whatever was not brought, is sent calf's-foot jelly and ends up with prisms in her window. Jimmy Bean, a ten-year-old with no home, discovers that the Ladies' Aid back West would rather spend money on a little boy in India, because the boy in India counts in their report. John Pendleton, the recluse of the big grey house, is found in Pendleton Woods with a broken leg, and asks Pollyanna to come and live with him because he once loved her mother. Even the minister, Reverend Paul Ford, sitting in the woods with a resignation half-written, is turned round by her father's eight hundred rejoicing texts.

Then an automobile knocks her down in the road, and the doctors say she may never walk again. For the first time Pollyanna cannot find anything to be glad about, and the book quietly turns itself over: one after another the townspeople come to Aunt Polly's door to say what the game has done for them, because the child who taught it can no longer play it. Aunt Polly, who has refused for fifteen years to be in the same room as Dr. Chilton, sends for him at last, and he knows of a specialist. The last chapter is a letter: Pollyanna has walked six steps, Aunt Polly has married Dr. Chilton beside her bed, and she is glad she lost her legs for a while, because you never know how lovely legs are until you haven't got them.

questions.prompt: When Pollyanna arrives, where does Aunt Polly decide she will sleep?

options: In the bare little room up in the attic
In the best bedroom on the ground floor
In the room next to Aunt Polly's own
In the small house at the end of the garden

questions.explanation: No pictures, no carpet, no looking-glass, and a long flight of stairs. Porter puts the room in early because it tells the reader exactly what kind of welcome this is, long before Aunt Polly says a single unkind word out loud.

questions.prompt: The glad game began with a missionary barrel. Pollyanna had asked for a doll, and what came in the barrel instead was a pair of ___.
questions.explanation: Her father told her to be glad she did not need them, and that was the first move of the game. It matters that the game starts with a real disappointment and not with something pleasant — the whole book depends on the game having been invented for hard things.

questions.prompt: On her first evening in the attic room, Pollyanna finds one thing to be glad about: there is no looking-glass. Why is she glad about that?

options: Then she cannot see her own freckles
Then she will not be vain about dresses
Then the room feels larger than it is
Then she has more space for her books

questions.explanation: She has been crying about her father a moment earlier — Nancy finds her on the floor. The freckles are the book's demonstration of how the game actually works: it does not deny that the room is bare, it finds one small true thing inside the bareness.

questions.prompt: Why does Aunt Polly take Pollyanna into her house at all?

options: She believes it is her duty, and says so
She has always wanted a child in the house
Pollyanna's father asked her to in a letter
The Ladies' Aid back West arranged it all

questions.explanation: She says it out loud, more than once, and it is not meant to be charming. Porter is careful to make Aunt Polly correct rather than cruel: she feeds and clothes her niece exactly as duty requires, and gives her nothing at all that duty does not.

questions.prompt: Put these events from Pollyanna's year in the town in the order they happen.

items: Pollyanna arrives and is given the attic room
She takes calf's-foot jelly to Mrs. Snow
She meets Jimmy Bean, who has no home
She finds Mr. Pendleton in the woods with a broken leg
She tells the minister about the rejoicing texts
An automobile knocks her down in the road
Aunt Polly at last sends for Dr. Chilton

questions.explanation: The order is the argument. Every person in the first half is someone Pollyanna gives the game to, and the accident in the second half is what forces all of them to give it back. Nothing in the last chapters would work if the visits had not come first.

questions.prompt: Match each person in the town to who they are in Pollyanna's story.

right: The servant who learns the game first
The gardener who knew Pollyanna's mother
The invalid who is never satisfied
The recluse who once loved her mother

questions.explanation: Four adults, and not one of them is happy when Pollyanna meets them. Notice how differently each one is reached: Nancy by example, Old Tom by memory, Mrs. Snow by jelly and prisms, and Mr. Pendleton by a broken leg and a great deal of stubbornness.

questions.prompt: People often describe the glad game wrongly. Sort each item into the right group.

content.groupA: What the glad game really asks you to do
content.groupB: What the glad game does not ask you to do

options.label: Look for one thing to be glad about
Keep playing even when it is hard
Say the glad thing out loud to someone
Pretend that nothing bad has happened
Tell other people they must be glad

questions.explanation: The right-hand column is what people who have not read the book assume the game is. Pollyanna cries in the attic on her first night, she admits outright that some things are hard to find gladness in, and after the accident she cannot play at all — the book itself rules out every item in group B.

questions.prompt: Pollyanna writes to the Ladies' Aid back West to ask them to help Jimmy Bean, who has no home. They would rather spend the money on a little boy in India. Why?

options: The boy in India counts in their report
They have never once heard of Jimmy Bean
Jimmy Bean is too old for their charity
They spent all their money on the barrel

questions.explanation: Pollyanna's reply is the sharpest line in the book: she says she would rather see Jimmy Bean grow than a report. Porter puts genuinely good people in the wrong here — the Ladies' Aid are not villains, they are simply keeping score, and a real child loses out because of it.

questions.prompt: What happens to Pollyanna near the end of the book?

options: She is hit by an automobile and cannot walk
She falls from the attic window one night
She catches the fever that killed her father
She is thrown from Timothy's open buggy

questions.explanation: It happens in the road, in one sentence, with no warning at all — and the doctors think she may never walk again. Up to this point the book has been a comedy about a cheerful child; from here on it is about whether the game is worth anything when the person who invented it needs it herself.

questions.prompt: After the accident Pollyanna cannot find anything to be glad about. What happens then?

options: The town comes to tell her what it did for them
Aunt Polly forbids anyone to mention the game
Nancy writes down a new rule for the game
She invents a second, harder game instead

questions.explanation: One after another they arrive at Aunt Polly's door — Mrs. Snow, the minister, Mr. Pendleton, people Pollyanna barely remembers — to say what the game has done for them. This is the point of the whole book: she stops being able to play, so everyone she taught plays it for her.

questions.prompt: The last chapter is a letter in which Pollyanna writes that she has walked six steps, and that Aunt Polly got married right beside her bed to Dr. ___.
questions.explanation: Aunt Polly had refused to be in the same room as him for fifteen years, after a quarrel neither of them would mention. Pollyanna's accident is what ends it: Aunt Polly sends for him because he is the best doctor, and he turns out to know of a specialist who can help.

questions.prompt: Some people say the glad game teaches a child to pretend that hard things are fine. Others say it is a way of surviving them. Using what actually happens to Pollyanna in the book — including the accident — which do you think it is? Explain your answer.
questions.explanation: Both positions can earn full marks, but the strong version of either one uses the book. Evidence that it is survival: it was invented over a pair of crutches, Pollyanna cries in the attic and plays it anyway, and she never once tells anyone their trouble is small. Evidence for the other side: she plays it at Mrs. Snow when Mrs. Snow is genuinely ill, and after the accident the game fails her completely and other people have to carry it. Accept any clear position argued from events in the book.

questions.prompt: Pollyanna finds a glad thing for everyone she visits. Invent one new person in the town for her to visit: who are they, what has gone wrong for them, and what is the one glad thing Pollyanna finds? It must be something small and true, not a promise that everything will get better.
questions.explanation: There is no single right answer, and the last sentence of the question is the whole test. Pollyanna never tells anybody their trouble will pass; she finds a thing that is already true — no looking-glass, so no freckles. An invention that comforts by promising a happy ending is not the glad game.
